The following description:

- **Transformation format**  
  "For a standard load instruction that is not a compressed instruction and is one of LB, LBU, LH, LHU, LW, LWU, LD, FLW, FLD, FLQ, or FLH, the transformed instruction has the format shown in Figure 121."

- **Figure 121 description**  
  "Figure 121. Transformed load instruction (LB, LBU, LH, LHU, LW, LWU, LD, FLW, FLD, FLQ, or FLH). **Fields funct3, rd, and opcode are the same as the trapping load instruction.**"

- **Immediate‑offset handling in transformed basic loads**  
  "Note also that, for basic loads and stores, the transformations replace the instruction's immediate offset fields with zero."  

- **Bit‑pattern of transformed standard instructions**  
  "Bits 1:0 of a transformed standard instruction will be binary 01 if the trapping instruction is compressed and 11 if not."  

- **Decoding requirement for LB in mtinst/htinst**  
  "In decoding the contents of mtinst or htinst, once software has determined that the register contains the encoding of a standard basic load (LB, LBU, LH, LHU, LW, LWU, LD, FLW, FLD, FLQ, or FLH) or basic store (SB, SH, SW, SD, FSW, FSD, FSQ, or FSH), it is not necessary to confirm also that the immediate offset fields (31:25, and 24:20 or 11:7) are zeros."
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: A non‑compressed standard load instruction whose mnemonic is LB must be transformed into an instruction that follows the format defined in Figure 121.  
RULE 2: In the transformed LB instruction, the funct3, rd, and opcode fields must be identical to those of the original trapping LB instruction.  
RULE 3: When an LB instruction is transformed, all immediate offset fields of the original instruction are replaced with zero in the transformed encoding.  
RULE 4: For a transformed LB instruction, bits 1:0 are 01 if the original trapping LB instruction was compressed and are 11 if the original trapping LB instruction was not compressed.  
RULE 5: When decoding the contents of mtinst or htinst that contain an LB encoding, software may assume the immediate offset fields are zero and does not need to verify that they are zero.

The following description:

- Pointer masking **applies** to all explicit memory accesses. In the Base and Privileged ISAs the set of explicit memory accesses includes **LB**.  

- Pointer masking **applies** to accesses generated by instructions on the CPU (including CPU extensions such as an FPU). Therefore a load byte (LB) instruction is subject to pointer masking.  

- **Misaligned accesses are supported**, subject to the same limitations as in the absence of pointer masking. The behavior is identical to applying the pointer‑masking transformation to every constituent aligned memory access; i.e., the bytes accessed by an LB instruction are the same bytes that would be accessed if the pointer‑masking transformation were applied to each byte of the access without pointer masking.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: The effective address used by an LB instruction is transformed by pointer masking before the memory access is performed.  
RULE 2: An LB instruction executed by any CPU instruction, including those from extensions such as an FPU, is subject to pointer masking.  
RULE 3: An LB instruction must correctly handle misaligned address operands, subject to the same architectural limitations that apply when pointer masking is not performed.  
RULE 4: When an LB instruction accesses a misaligned address, the byte fetched shall be the same as the byte that would be fetched if the pointer‑masking transformation were applied separately to each aligned byte of the access without pointer masking.

The following description:

- **Encoding and addressing**  
  Loads are encoded in the I‑type format. The effective address for an LBU is obtained by adding register rs1 to the sign‑extended 12‑bit offset.

- **Definition of LBU**  
  "LB and LBU are defined analogously for 8‑bit values."  

- **Exception behavior**  
  Loads with a destination of **x0** must still raise any exceptions and cause any other side effects even though the load value is discarded.  

- **Alignment requirements**  
  Naturally aligned loads shall not raise an address‑misaligned exception. (Since LBU accesses a single byte, any address is naturally aligned.)

- **Misaligned access handling**  
  Loads whose effective address is not naturally aligned to the referenced datatype (i.e., the effective address is not divisible by the size of the access in bytes) have behavior dependent on the EEI.

- **Endianness guarantee**  
  In a system for which endianness is byte‑address invariant, the following property holds: if a byte is stored to memory at some address in some endianness, then a byte‑sized load from that address in any endianness returns the stored value. This applies to LBU.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: LBU computes its effective memory address by adding the contents of register rs1 to the sign‑extended 12‑bit immediate offset encoded in the I‑type instruction.  

RULE 2: LBU loads an unsigned 8‑bit value from the effective address and zero‑extends the value to the processor's XLEN width.  

RULE 3: When the destination register rd of an LBU is x0, the instruction must still raise any load‑related exceptions and must still perform any side effects even though the loaded value is discarded.  

RULE 4: LBU must not raise an address‑misaligned exception for any effective address because a byte access is naturally aligned for all addresses.  

RULE 5: If the effective address used by an LBU is not naturally aligned to the byte size, the resulting behavior is determined by the execution‑environment interface (EEI).  

RULE 6: In a system whose endianness is byte‑address invariant, an LBU performed at an address that previously stored a byte returns exactly the stored byte value, independent of the system's endianness.

The following description:

- LBU is a **standard load instruction** (non‑compressed) that is listed among the loads for which a transformed instruction may be written to the trap‑instruction CSR (mtinst or htinst) when a synchronous exception occurs.  
  - Table 55 shows that for the exceptions **Load address misaligned**, **Load access fault**, **Load page fault**, and **Load guest‑page fault** the entry "Transformed Standard Instruction" is **Yes**; therefore a trapping LBU may cause the hardware to write a transformed LBU encoding to the trap‑instruction register.

- **Transformed load‑instruction format (Figure 121)** applies to LBU:  
  - The fields **funct3**, **rd**, and **opcode** in the transformed encoding are **the same as the trapping LBU instruction**.  
  - The **Addr. Offset** field (which replaces the original rs1 field in bits 19:15) is **the positive difference between the faulting virtual address (written to mtval or stval) and the original virtual address**.  
  - For basic loads, **the transformation replaces the instruction's immediate offset fields with zero**.  
  - Consequently, for a non‑compressed LBU the transformed encoding has bits 1:0 equal to **11** (bits 1:0 are **01** only if the trapping instruction is compressed).

- When software decodes the contents of mtinst or htinst:  
  - If the register value is recognized as the encoding of a **standard basic load** (including LBU) the software **does not need to verify that the immediate offset fields (31:25, and 24:20 or 11:7) are zeros**; the knowledge that the value is a basic‑load encoding is sufficient to prove that the trapping instruction was an LBU of the same kind.

- The transformation rules for LBU are subject to the same forward‑compatibility requirements as other loads: a future version of the standard may add information to fields that are currently zero, but such information is **performance‑only** and may be safely ignored.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: LBU is a standard non‑compressed load instruction that may cause a transformed instruction to be written to the trap‑instruction CSR mtinst or htinst when a synchronous exception occurs.  
RULE 2: When a synchronous exception of type load address misaligned, load access fault, load page fault, or load guest‑page fault is raised by an LBU, the hardware MAY write a transformed LBU encoding to mtinst or htinst.  
RULE 3: In the transformed encoding of an LBU, the funct3, rd, and opcode fields MUST be identical to those of the trapping LBU instruction.  
RULE 4: In the transformed encoding of an LBU, the Addr. Offset field (bits 19:15) MUST contain the positive difference between the faulting virtual address recorded in mtval or stval and the original virtual address used by the trapping LBU.  
RULE 5: When an LBU is transformed as a basic load, the immediate offset fields of the original instruction MUST be set to zero in the transformed encoding.  
RULE 6: The transformed encoding of a non‑compressed LBU MUST have bits 1:0 equal to 11.  
RULE 7: Software decoding mtinst or htinst may determine that a trapping LBU occurred without verifying that the immediate offset fields (31:25, 24:20, or 11:7) are zero, provided the register value is recognized as a standard basic‑load encoding.  
RULE 8: Implementations MUST treat any non‑zero bits that future extensions may place in fields currently zero by the LBU transformation as performance‑only information that may be ignored without affecting architectural behavior.

The following description:

- **LBU is an explicit memory access subject to pointer masking**  
  The Base Instruction Set list of explicit memory accesses includes LBU:  

  ```
  Base Instruction Set : LB, LH, LW, LBU, LHU, LWU, LD, SB, SH, SW, SD.
  ```

- **Pointer masking applies to LBU**  
  The specification states that "Pointer masking applies to all explicit memory accesses." Because LBU is an explicit memory access, pointer masking is applied to the address used by an LBU instruction when pointer masking is enabled for the privilege mode that performs the access.

- **Misaligned LBU accesses**  
  "Misaligned accesses are supported, subject to the same limitations as in the absence of pointer masking. The behavior is identical to applying the pointer masking transformation to every constituent aligned memory access." Therefore, a misaligned LBU load accesses the same bytes that would be accessed if the pointer‑masking transformation were applied individually to each byte of the access.

- **No exemption for LBU**  
  The text explicitly notes that pointer masking is **not** applied to SFENCE.*, HFENCE.*, SINVAL.*, or HINVAL.*. LBU is not listed among these exemptions, so pointer masking applies to LBU.

- **Effect of privilege‑mode settings**  
  "MPRV and SPVP affect pointer masking as well, causing the pointer masking settings of the effective privilege mode to be applied." Consequently, when an LBU executes under MPRV or SPVP, the pointer‑masking settings of the effective privilege mode are used.  

  "When MXR is in effect at the effective privilege mode where explicit memory access is performed, pointer masking does not apply." Hence, if MXR is active in the effective privilege mode, an LBU load is *not* subject to pointer masking.  

  "Note that this includes cases where page‑based virtual memory is not in effect; i.e., although MXR has no effect on permissions checks when page‑based virtual memory is not in effect, it is still used in determining whether or not pointer masking should be applied." Thus, the presence or absence of page‑based virtual memory does not change the applicability of pointer masking to LBU, except as mediated by MXR.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: LBU is classified as an explicit memory access in the Base Instruction Set list.  
RULE 2: Because LBU is an explicit memory access, the address used by an LBU must be transformed by pointer masking when pointer masking is enabled for the privilege mode that performs the access.  
RULE 3: Pointer masking is excluded only for SFENCE.*, HFENCE.*, SINVAL.*, and HINVAL.*, and since LBU is not listed among these exclusions, pointer masking applies to LBU.  
RULE 4: Misaligned LBU accesses are supported and the bytes loaded are identical to those that would be accessed if the pointer‑masking transformation were applied individually to each aligned constituent byte of the access.  
RULE 5: When an LBU executes while MPRV or SPVP is active, the pointer‑masking settings of the effective privilege mode must be used for the address transformation of the LBU.  
RULE 6: If MXR is in effect at the effective privilege mode where an LBU is performed, pointer masking must not be applied to the LBU address.  
RULE 7: The presence or absence of page‑based virtual memory does not affect whether pointer masking applies to an LBU, except that MXR determines the applicability of pointer masking.

The following description:

The **ld.{aq,aqrl}** instruction atomically loads a **2 width -byte** value from the address in **rs1** and places the sign‑extended value into the register **rd**, subject to the ordering annotations specified in the instruction.

- **Mnemonic**: `ld.{aq,aqrl} rd , ( rs1 )`  

- **Description**  
  - This instruction loads **2 width** bytes of memory from **rs1** atomically and writes the result into **rd**.  
  - If the size (**2 width+3**) is less than **XLEN**, it is sign‑extended to fill the destination register.  
  - This load **must have** the ordering annotation **aq** and **may have** ordering annotation **rl** encoded in the instruction.  
  - The instruction always has an **"acquire‑RCsc"** annotation, and if the bit **rl** is set the instruction has a **"release‑RCsc"** annotation.  

- **Architectural constraints**  
  - The versions without the **aq** bit set are **RESERVED**.  
  - **LD.{AQ, AQRL}** is **RV64‑only**.  

- **Rationale** (informative)  
  - The **aq** bit is mandatory because the two encodings that would be produced are not seen as useful at this time.  
  - The version with neither the **aq** nor the **rl** bit set would correspond to a load with no ordering annotations that was guaranteed to be performed atomically; this can be achieved with ordinary load instructions by suitably aligning pointers.  
  - The version with only the **rl** bit would correspond to **load‑release**. Load‑release has theoretical applications in seqlocks, but is not supported in language‑level memory models and so is not included.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: LD.{aq,aqrl} atomically loads a 2‑width‑byte value from the memory address contained in rs1 and writes the result into rd.  
RULE 2: If the size of the value loaded by LD.{aq,aqrl} (2 width+3 bytes) is less than XLEN, the loaded value is sign‑extended to fill the destination register rd.  
RULE 3: LD.{aq,aqrl} MUST have the acquire (aq) ordering annotation encoded in the instruction.  
RULE 4: LD.{aq,aqrl} MAY have the release (rl) ordering annotation encoded in the instruction.  
RULE 5: LD.{aq,aqrl} always has an acquire‑RCsc annotation, and when the rl bit is set the instruction additionally has a release‑RCsc annotation.  
RULE 6: Encodings of LD.{aq,aqrl} in which the aq bit is not set are RESERVED and have no defined architectural behavior.  
RULE 7: LD.{aq,aqrl} is defined only for RV64 implementations and is not defined for RV32.

The following description:

- The pseudocode for the **cm.pop** instruction includes the following clause:

```
if (XLEN== 32 ) bytes= 4 ; else bytes= 8 ;
```

- When `bytes` equals 8, the following assembly operation is performed for each register in `xreg_list`:

```
asm("ld x[i], 0(addr)");
```

- In the same pseudocode, the address used for the load is defined as:

```
addr = sp + stack_adj - bytes;
```

- After each execution of the `ld` instruction, the address is updated with:

```
addr -= bytes;
```

These statements together specify that, in the context of the **cm.pop** operation, the `ld` instruction loads a double‑word (8 bytes) from the memory location given by `addr` into the destination register `x[i]`, where `addr` is computed as `sp + stack_adj - 8` and is decremented by 8 after each load.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: When executing the cm.pop operation, the implementation shall set bytes to 4 if XLEN equals 32, otherwise shall set bytes to 8.  
RULE 2: When bytes equals 8 during the cm.pop operation, the implementation shall execute an LD instruction that loads from address addr with offset 0 into register x[i] for each register in xreg_list.  
RULE 3: During the cm.pop operation, the address used by the LD instruction shall be computed as sp plus stack_adj minus bytes.  
RULE 4: After each execution of the LD instruction in the cm.pop operation, the address value shall be decremented by bytes.  
RULE 5: Each LD instruction executed by the cm.pop operation shall load a double‑word (8 bytes) from the memory location given by addr into the destination register x[i]; the initial addr is sp plus stack_adj minus 8 and is decremented by 8 after each load.

- The **LD** instruction is used in the cm.popret operation to load an 8‑byte (doubleword) value from memory into a register:

The following description:

ld rd, offset(rs1)   Load doubleword to register pair, 32-bit encoding  

As the access size is 64-bit, accesses are only considered naturally aligned for effective addresses that are a multiple of 8.  

In this case, these instructions are guaranteed to not raise an address-misaligned exception.  

Even if naturally aligned, the memory access might not be performed atomically.  

If the effective address is a multiple of 4, then each word access is required to be performed atomically.  

**Required behavior summary**

| Alignment | Word accesses guaranteed atomic? | Can cause misaligned trap? |
|-----------|-----------------------------------|----------------------------|
| 8 B       | yes                               | no                         |
| 4 B not 8 B| yes                              | yes                        |
| else      | no                                | yes                        |

To ensure resumable trap handling is possible for the load instructions, the base register **must** have its original value if a trap is taken.  

The other register in the pair can have been updated.  

This affects x2 for the stack pointer relative instruction and rs1 otherwise.  

If an implementation performs a doubleword load access atomically and the register file implements write‑back for even/odd register pairs, the mentioned atomicity requirements are inherently fulfilled.  

Otherwise, an implementation either needs to delay the write‑back until the write can be performed atomically, or order sequential writes to the registers to ensure the requirement above is satisfied.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: LD loads a 64‑bit doubleword from memory into a pair of registers specified by the destination register field.  
RULE 2: For LD, an effective address that is a multiple of 8 bytes is considered naturally aligned.  
RULE 3: LD must not raise an address‑misaligned exception when its effective address is a multiple of 8 bytes.  
RULE 4: LD may perform a non‑atomic memory access even when the effective address is naturally aligned.  
RULE 5: LD must perform each 32‑bit word access atomically when its effective address is a multiple of 4 bytes.  
RULE 6: When the effective address of LD is a multiple of 8 bytes, the word accesses are guaranteed to be atomic and no misaligned trap may be raised.  
RULE 7: When the effective address of LD is a multiple of 4 bytes but not a multiple of 8 bytes, each word access is guaranteed to be atomic and a misaligned trap may be raised.  
RULE 8: When the effective address of LD is not a multiple of 4 bytes, the word accesses are not guaranteed to be atomic and a misaligned trap may be raised.  
RULE 9: If LD takes a trap, the architectural value of the base register (rs1) must remain unchanged.  
RULE 10: If LD takes a trap, the registers in the destination pair may have been updated partially or fully.  
RULE 11: When LD uses a stack‑pointer‑relative address, the base register that must retain its original value on a trap is x2; otherwise the base register is rs1.  
RULE 12: If an implementation performs the doubleword memory access of LD atomically and writes back the destination register pair atomically, the required per‑word atomicity is inherently satisfied.  
RULE 13: If an implementation does not perform the doubleword access of LD atomically, it must either delay the write‑back to the destination registers until an atomic write can be performed or order the sequential writes to the registers so that the required per‑word atomicity is satisfied.
====================================================== END - 835 =======================================================

The following description:

- For the purposes of RVWMO and exception handling, **LD** (and SD) instructions are considered misaligned loads (and stores).  

- An **LD** instruction whose effective address is a multiple of 4 **gives rise to two 4‑byte memory operations**.  

- The definition permits **LD** instructions to give rise to exactly one memory access, regardless of alignment.  

- If an **LD** instruction has a 4‑byte‑aligned effective address and is decomposed into two 32‑bit operations:  
  * **There is no constraint on the order in which the operations are performed**.  
  * **Each operation is guaranteed to be atomic**.  
  * **These decomposed sequences are interruptible**.  

- **Exceptions might occur on subsequent operations**, making the effects of previous operations within the same instruction visible.  

- **Software should make no assumptions about the number or order of accesses these instructions might give rise to, beyond the 4‑byte constraint mentioned above**.

=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: For RVWMO and exception handling, an LD instruction is treated as a misaligned load.  
RULE 2: If the effective address of an LD instruction is a multiple of 4, the instruction must generate two 4‑byte memory operations.  
RULE 3: An LD instruction is permitted to generate exactly one memory access regardless of the alignment of its effective address.  
RULE 4: When an LD instruction with a 4‑byte‑aligned effective address is decomposed into two 32‑bit operations, the implementation imposes no constraint on the order in which the two operations are performed.  
RULE 5: Each of the two 32‑bit operations produced by a decomposed LD instruction with a 4‑byte‑aligned effective address is guaranteed to be atomic.  
RULE 6: The sequence of two 32‑bit operations generated by a decomposed LD instruction with a 4‑byte‑aligned effective address may be interrupted.  
RULE 7: If an exception occurs on a later memory operation of an LD instruction, the architectural effects of any earlier memory operation of the same instruction become visible.  
RULE 8: Software must not assume any specific number or order of memory accesses generated by an LD instruction beyond the requirement that each access be 4 bytes in size.

The following description:

LD is a **standard load instruction** that is **not a compressed instruction** and is listed among the load instructions
`LB, LBU, LH, LHU, LW, LWU, LD, FLW, FLD, FLQ, or FLH`.

* For such a standard LD instruction, the **transformed instruction** written to the trap‑instruction CSR (mtinst or htinst) **has the format shown in Figure 121**.  
  – *Fields* `funct3`, `rd`, and `opcode` **are the same as the trapping load instruction**.  

* In all transformed instructions of this class (including LD), the **Addr. Offset field** that replaces the instruction's `rs1` field in bits 19:15 **is the positive difference between the faulting virtual address (written to mtval or stval) and the original virtual address**.  
  – This difference **can be non‑zero only for a misaligned memory access**.  
  – For basic loads (including LD), the transformation **replaces the instruction's immediate offset fields with zero**.

* When decoding the contents of mtinst or htinst, once software has determined that the register contains the encoding of a **basic load** (which includes LD), **it is not necessary to confirm that the immediate offset fields (31:25, and 24:20 or 11:7) are zeros**; the knowledge that the value is the encoding of a basic load/store **is sufficient to prove that the trapping instruction is of the same kind**.

* **Bits 1:0 of a transformed standard instruction** are **binary 11** if the trapping instruction is **not compressed** (as is the case for LD).

* Table 57 maps the **special pseudoinstruction value** used for a 64‑bit VS‑stage read to the encoding of LD:

```
Encoding   Instruction
0x00003003 ld x0,0(x0)
```

Thus the **binary encoding** of an LD instruction that serves as the pseudoinstruction for a 64‑bit VS‑stage read is `0x00003003`.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: LD is a standard (non‑compressed) load instruction listed among LB, LBU, LH, LHU, LW, LWU, LD, FLW, FLD, FLQ, and FLH.  
RULE 2: When a standard LD instruction traps, the transformed instruction written to the trap‑instruction CSR (mtinst or htinst) must have the same funct3, rd, and opcode fields as the original LD.  
RULE 3: In the transformed LD stored in mtinst or htinst, the Addr.Offset field (bits 19:15) must equal the positive difference between the faulting virtual address (written to mtval or stval) and the original virtual address.  
RULE 4: The Addr.Offset field of the transformed LD may be non‑zero only when the faulting memory access was misaligned.  
RULE 5: For a basic load such as LD, the transformation must replace all immediate offset fields in the encoded instruction with zeros.  
RULE 6: The two low‑order bits (bits 1:0) of the transformed LD in mtinst or htinst must be binary 11 because the original LD is not compressed.  
RULE 7: The 32‑bit encoding 0x00003003 represents the LD x0,0(x0) pseudoinstruction used for a 64‑bit VS‑stage read.

- **Pointer masking applies to LD when the instruction is executed on the CPU** (including CPU extensions such as an FPU).  
  "Pointer masking only applies to accesses generated by instructions on the CPU …"

- **MPRV and SPVP affect pointer masking for LD** by causing the pointer‑masking settings of the *effective* privilege mode to be applied.  
  "MPRV and SPVP affect pointer masking as well, causing the pointer masking settings of the effective privilege mode to be applied."

- **When MXR is in effect at the effective privilege mode where the LD is performed, pointer masking does *not* apply**.  
  "When MXR is in effect at the effective privilege mode where explicit memory access is performed, pointer masking does not apply."

- **If page‑based virtual memory is not in effect, MXR still determines whether pointer masking is applied to LD** (MXR has no effect on permission checks in that case, but it is still used to decide on pointer masking).  
  "Note that this includes cases where page‑based virtual memory is not in effect; i.e., although MXR has no effect on permissions checks when page‑based virtual memory is not in effect, it is still used in determining whether or not pointer masking should be applied."

- **Misaligned LD accesses are supported**, with the same limitations as in the absence of pointer masking. The accessed bytes must be identical to those that would be accessed if the pointer‑masking transformation were applied individually to each byte of the access.  
  "Misaligned accesses are supported, subject to the same limitations as in the absence of pointer masking. The behavior is identical to applying the pointer masking transformation to every constituent aligned memory access. In other words, the accessed bytes should be identical to the bytes that would be accessed if the pointer masking transformation was individually applied to every byte of the access without pointer masking."
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: LD is an explicit memory access and therefore must be subject to the pointer‑masking transformation defined for explicit memory accesses.  
RULE 2: When an LD instruction is executed on the CPU, including when generated by CPU extensions such as an FPU, pointer masking must be applied to the effective address.  
RULE 3: If MPRV or SPVP is enabled, LD must apply pointer masking using the pointer‑masking settings of the effective privilege mode.  
RULE 4: When MXR is set in the effective privilege mode at which an LD is performed, pointer masking must not be applied to that LD.  
RULE 5: Even when page‑based virtual memory is not in effect, MXR must be consulted to determine whether pointer masking is applied to an LD.  
RULE 6: LD must support misaligned accesses, subject to the same architectural limitations that apply when pointer masking is not present.  
RULE 7: The bytes accessed by a misaligned LD must be identical to the bytes that would be accessed if the pointer‑masking transformation were applied individually to each byte of the access.

The following description:

- **Encoding and address calculation**  
  - LH is a load instruction and therefore is encoded in the I‑type format.  
  - The effective address for LH is obtained by adding the contents of register rs1 to the sign‑extended 12‑bit offset.

- **Operation**  
  - "LH loads a 16‑bit value from memory, then sign‑extends to 32‑bits before storing in rd."  
  - The loaded value is transferred from memory to register rd; the lower 16 bits are taken from memory and sign‑extended to fill the full 32‑bit destination register.

- **Exception behavior**  
  - "Loads with a destination of x0 must still raise any exceptions and cause any other side effects even though the load value is discarded."  
  - "Regardless of EEI, loads … whose effective addresses are naturally aligned shall not raise an address‑misaligned exception." (applies to LH because its natural alignment is 2 bytes).  
  - For misaligned effective addresses (addresses not divisible by 2), the behavior is EEI‑dependent: the access may complete successfully, or it may raise an address‑misaligned exception or an access‑fault exception, as defined by the EEI.

- **Interaction with the execution environment (EEI)**  
  - The EEI defines whether misaligned LH accesses are supported invisibly, raise a contained trap, or cause a fatal trap.  
  - When misaligned accesses are supported, they may be handled in hardware, via an invisible trap, or by a combination of both, and their performance may vary.  
  - Misaligned LH accesses are not guaranteed to be atomic; additional synchronization may be required to ensure atomicity.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: LH is encoded using the I-type format.  
RULE 2: The effective address for LH is computed by adding the contents of register rs1 to the sign-extended 12-bit immediate offset.  
RULE 3: LH loads a 16-bit value from memory, sign‑extends it to 32 bits, and writes the result to register rd.  
RULE 4: When the destination register rd of an LH instruction is x0, the load still raises any applicable exceptions and performs any other side effects even though the loaded value is discarded.  
RULE 5: If the effective address of an LH instruction is naturally aligned (divisible by 2), the instruction shall not raise an address‑misaligned exception regardless of the execution environment implementation.  
RULE 6: If the effective address of an LH instruction is not divisible by 2, the behavior is execution‑environment‑implementation dependent and may either complete successfully, raise an address‑misaligned exception, or raise an access‑fault exception.  
RULE 7: The execution environment defines whether misaligned LH accesses are supported invisibly, cause a contained trap, or cause a fatal trap.  
RULE 8: When misaligned LH accesses are supported by the execution environment, they may be handled entirely in hardware, via an invisible trap, or by a combination of both, and their performance may vary.  
RULE 9: Misaligned LH accesses are not guaranteed to be atomic, so additional synchronization may be required to ensure atomicity.

The following description:

The load‑acquire instruction **lh.{aq,aqrl}** atomically loads a 2‑width‑byte value from the address in `rs1` and places the sign‑extended value into the register `rd`, subject to the ordering annotations specified in the instruction.

- This instruction loads 2 width bytes of memory from `rs1` atomically and writes the result into `rd`.  
- If the size (2 width+3) is less than XLEN, it **is sign‑extended** to fill the destination register.  
- This load **must have** the ordering annotation `aq` **and may have** ordering annotation `rl` encoded in the instruction.  
- The instruction **always has** an "acquire‑RCsc" annotation, and **if the bit rl is set the instruction has** a "release‑RCsc" annotation.  

Additional encoding constraints:

- The versions without the `aq` bit set **are RESERVED**.  
- The `aq` bit **is mandatory** because the two encodings that would be produced are not seen as useful at this time.  
- The version with neither the `aq` nor the `rl` bit set would correspond to a load with no ordering annotations that was guaranteed to be performed atomically; this can be achieved with ordinary load instructions by suitably aligning pointers.  
- The version with only the `rl` bit would correspond to load‑release; load‑release **is not supported** in language‑level memory models and so is not included.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: LH.{aq,aqrl} atomically loads a 2‑byte value from the address in rs1 and places the sign‑extended result into rd.  
RULE 2: LH sign‑extends the loaded 2‑byte value to XLEN when the loaded size is less than XLEN.  
RULE 3: LH must have the ordering annotation aq encoded in the instruction.  
RULE 4: LH may have the ordering annotation rl encoded in the instruction.  
RULE 5: LH always has an acquire‑RCsc annotation.  
RULE 6: If the rl bit of LH is set, LH also has a release‑RCsc annotation.  
RULE 7: Encodings of LH without the aq bit set are RESERVED.  
RULE 8: The aq bit of LH is mandatory.  
RULE 9: The functionality of an atomic load without ordering annotations can be achieved with ordinary load instructions by suitably aligning pointers, not with an LH encoding.  
RULE 10: Encodings of LH with only the rl bit set (load‑release) are not supported.

The following description:

The following description:

- **Operation**: "LHU loads a 16-bit value from memory but then zero extends to 32‑bits before storing in rd."  

- **Load semantics**: "Loads copy a value from memory to register rd."  

- **Address calculation**: "The effective address is obtained by adding register rs1 to the sign‑extended 12‑bit offset."  

- **Destination‑x0 behavior**: "Loads with a destination of x0 must still raise any exceptions and cause any other side effects even though the load value is discarded."  

- **Alignment exception rule**: "Loads and stores whose effective addresses are naturally aligned shall not raise an address‑misaligned exception."  

- **Misaligned‑access behavior**: "Loads and stores whose effective address is not naturally aligned to the referenced datatype (i.e., the effective address is not divisible by the size of the access in bytes) have behavior dependent on the EEI."  

- **Endianness – byte‑address invariant property**: "In a system for which endianness is byte‑address invariant, the following property holds: if a byte is stored to memory at some address in some endianness, then a byte‑sized load from that address in any endianness returns the stored value."  

- **Little‑endian multibyte load**: "In a little‑endian configuration, multibyte loads transfer the contents of the lesser memory byte addresses to the less‑significant register bytes."  

- **Big‑endian multibyte load**: "In a big‑endian configuration, multibyte loads transfer the contents of the greater memory byte addresses to the less‑significant register bytes."  

- **Atomicity of aligned loads**: "Whereas naturally aligned loads and stores are guaranteed to execute atomically, misaligned loads and stores might not, and hence require additional synchronization to ensure atomicity."  

- **Legal address space**: "The EEI will define what portions of the address space are legal to access with which instructions (e.g., some addresses might be read only, or support word access only)."  

- **Endianness definition**: "The EEI will define whether the memory system is little‑endian or big‑endian. In RISC‑V, endianness is byte‑address invariant."  

- **EEI support for misaligned accesses**:  
  - "An EEI may guarantee that misaligned loads and stores are fully supported, and so the software running inside the execution environment will never experience a contained or fatal address‑misaligned trap."  
  - "An EEI may not guarantee misaligned loads and stores are handled invisibly. In this case, loads and stores that are not naturally aligned may either complete execution successfully or raise an exception. The exception raised can be either an address‑misaligned exception or an access‑fault exception."  
  - "When an EEI does not guarantee misaligned loads and stores are handled invisibly, the EEI must define if exceptions caused by address misalignment result in a contained trap (allowing software running inside the execution environment to handle the trap) or a fatal trap (terminating execution)."
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: LHU loads a 16‑bit value from memory and zero‑extends it to a 32‑bit value before writing the result to rd.  
RULE 2: LHU copies the loaded value from memory into the destination register rd.  
RULE 3: LHU computes its effective address by adding the contents of rs1 to the sign‑extended 12‑bit immediate offset.  
RULE 4: LHU with destination register x0 must still raise any exceptions and perform all side effects even though the loaded value is discarded.  
RULE 5: LHU whose effective address is naturally aligned (address divisible by 2) shall not raise an address‑misaligned exception.  
RULE 6: If LHU's effective address is not naturally aligned to a 2‑byte boundary, the resulting behavior is defined by the execution environment interface (EEI).  
RULE 7: In a byte‑address invariant system, each byte fetched by LHU reflects the value previously stored at its address independent of the system's endianness.  
RULE 8: In a little‑endian configuration, LHU places the byte from the lower memory address into the least‑significant bits of rd and the byte from the higher address into the next higher bits.  
RULE 9: In a big‑endian configuration, LHU places the byte from the higher memory address into the least‑significant bits of rd and the byte from the lower address into the next higher bits.  
RULE 10: When LHU is naturally aligned, its execution is atomic with respect to other memory operations.  
RULE 11: When LHU is misaligned, its execution may not be atomic and additional synchronization may be required to guarantee atomicity.  
RULE 12: The EEI defines which portions of the address space are legal for LHU to access, including any read‑only or word‑only restrictions.  
RULE 13: The EEI defines whether the memory system used by LHU is little‑endian or big‑endian, and RISC‑V requires that the endianness be byte‑address invariant.  
RULE 14: An EEI may guarantee that misaligned LHU accesses are fully supported, in which case software executing LHU will never encounter a contained or fatal address‑misaligned trap.  
RULE 15: An EEI may not guarantee invisible handling of misaligned LHU accesses, and in that case a misaligned LHU may either complete successfully or raise either an address‑misaligned exception or an access‑fault exception.  
RULE 16: When an EEI does not guarantee invisible handling of misaligned LHU, the EEI must specify whether exceptions caused by address misalignment result in a contained trap or a fatal trap.

RULE 4: The LHU instruction zero‑extends the loaded halfword to XLEN bits and writes the result to destination register rd′.  
RULE 5: The LHU instruction selects its destination register rd′ from the standard register set x8‑x15.  
RULE 6: The LHU instruction selects its source register rs1′ from the standard register set x8‑x15.  
RULE 7: The LHU instruction has no architectural prerequisites for execution.

The following description:

Pointer masking applies to all explicit memory accesses.  
- ⚫ Base Instruction Set : LB, LH, LW, LBU, **LHU**, LWU, LD, SB, SH, SW, SD.  

Therefore the LHU instruction is subject to pointer masking.

Misaligned accesses are supported, subject to the same limitations as in the absence of pointer masking.  
The behavior is identical to applying the pointer masking transformation to every constituent aligned memory access.  

Pointer masking only applies to accesses generated by instructions on the CPU (including CPU extensions such as an FPU).  

MPRV and SPVP affect pointer masking as well, causing the pointer masking settings of the effective privilege mode to be applied.  

When MXR is in effect at the effective privilege mode where explicit memory access is performed, pointer masking does not apply.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: The LHU instruction's explicit memory accesses are subject to pointer masking.  
RULE 2: When the LHU instruction generates a misaligned memory access, the operation is performed as if pointer masking is applied to each aligned sub‑access, and the same limitations that apply to misaligned accesses without pointer masking also apply.  
RULE 3: Pointer masking applies to LHU memory accesses only when the access is generated by an instruction executing on the CPU, including accesses generated by CPU extensions such as an FPU.  
RULE 4: If the MPRV or SPVP privilege‑mode settings are active, the pointer‑masking behavior of the LHU instruction follows the pointer‑masking configuration of the effective privilege mode.  
RULE 5: When MXR is active in the effective privilege mode that performs the LHU memory access, pointer masking does not apply to that LHU access.

The following description:

The LPAD instruction is encoded with a 20‑bit immediate value called the landing‑pad‑label (LPL) that is matched to the expected landing pad label stored in bits 31:12 of the x7 register.

When LPL is encoded as zero, the LPAD instruction does not perform the label check and in programs built with this single‑label mode of operation the indirect call/jump sites do not need to establish an expected landing pad label value in x7.

When the ELP state is LP_EXPECTED, the processor checks the next instruction in the instruction stream as follows:

* If the next instruction is not 4‑byte aligned, **or** is not an LPAD instruction, **or** the landing‑pad label encoded in the LPAD is not zero **and** does not match the expected landing pad label in bits 31:12 of the x7 register, then a software‑check exception (cause = 18) is raised with xtval set to "landing pad fault (code=2)".  
* Otherwise, the ELP state is updated to NO_LP_EXPECTED.

The LPAD requires a 4‑byte alignment to address the concatenation of two instructions A and B accidentally forming an unintended landing pad in the program.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: The LPAD instruction encodes a 20‑bit immediate called the landing‑pad‑label (LPL) which is compared with bits 31:12 of the x7 register.  
RULE 2: If the LPL field of an LPAD instruction is zero, the LPAD must not perform the label check and software may omit establishing an expected landing‑pad label value in x7.  
RULE 3: When the ELP state is LP_EXPECTED and the next instruction, which is expected to be an LPAD, is not 4‑byte aligned, the processor must raise a software‑check exception with cause 18 and xtval set to "landing pad fault (code=2)".  
RULE 4: When the ELP state is LP_EXPECTED and the next instruction is not an LPAD, the processor must raise a software‑check exception with cause 18 and xtval set to "landing pad fault (code=2)".  
RULE 5: When the ELP state is LP_EXPECTED and the next instruction is an LPAD whose LPL is non‑zero and does not equal bits 31:12 of x7, the processor must raise a software‑check exception with cause 18 and xtval set to "landing pad fault (code=2)".  
RULE 6: When the ELP state is LP_EXPECTED and the next instruction is a correctly aligned LPAD whose LPL is either zero or matches bits 31:12 of x7, the processor must update the ELP state to NO_LP_EXPECTED.  
RULE 7: The LPAD instruction must be placed at a 4‑byte aligned address; misaligned placement can cause the software‑check exception described for the LP_EXPECTED state.

The following description:

When Zicfilp is enabled, LPAD is the only instruction allowed to execute when the ELP state is **LP_EXPECTED**.  
If Zicfilp is not enabled then the instruction is a **no‑op**.

If Zicfilp is enabled, the LPAD instruction **causes a software‑check exception** with **xtval set to "landing pad fault (code=2)"** if any of the following conditions are true:

- The **pc is not 4‑byte aligned** and **ELP is LP_EXPECTED**.  
- The **ELP is LP_EXPECTED**, the **LPL is not zero**, and the **LPL does not match the expected landing pad label in bits 31:12 of the x7 register**.

If a software‑check exception is **not** caused, then **ELP is updated to NO_LP_EXPECTED**.

The operation of the LPAD instruction can be expressed as:

```
if (xLPE == 1 && ELP == LP_EXPECTED) {
    // If PC not 4‑byte aligned then software‑check exception
    if (pc[1:0] != 0) raise software‑check exception;
    // If landing pad label not matched -> software‑check exception
    else if (inst.LPL != x7[31:12] && inst.LPL != 0) raise software‑check exception;
    else ELP = NO_LP_EXPECTED;
} else {
    // No‑op
}
```
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: When Zicfilp is enabled and the architectural ELP state equals LP_EXPECTED, the LPAD instruction MUST be the only instruction that may be executed.  
RULE 2: When Zicfilp is not enabled, execution of the LPAD instruction MUST have no architectural effect (it is a no‑op).  
RULE 3: When Zicfilp is enabled and the LPAD instruction is executed while the PC is not 4‑byte aligned and the ELP state is LP_EXPECTED, the LPAD instruction MUST raise a software‑check exception with xtval set to "landing pad fault (code=2)".  
RULE 4: When Zicfilp is enabled and the LPAD instruction is executed while the ELP state is LP_EXPECTED, the LPL field of the instruction is non‑zero, and the LPL field does not equal bits 31:12 of the x7 register, the LPAD instruction MUST raise a software‑check exception with xtval set to "landing pad fault (code=2)".  
RULE 5: When Zicfilp is enabled and the LPAD instruction is executed while the ELP state is LP_EXPECTED, the PC is 4‑byte aligned, and either the LPL field is zero or it matches bits 31:12 of the x7 register, the LPAD instruction MUST update the architectural ELP state to NO_LP_EXPECTED and MUST NOT raise a software‑check exception.  
RULE 6: When Zicfilp is enabled and the ELP state is not LP_EXPECTED, execution of the LPAD instruction MUST have no architectural effect (it is a no‑op).

The following description:

- **Operation** – LR.D loads a doubleword from the address in `rs1`, places the value in `rd`, and registers a reservation set – a set of bytes that subsumes the bytes in the addressed doubleword.  

- **Availability** – LR.D is only available on RV64.  

- **Alignment requirement** – For LR (and SC), the address held in `rs1` *must* be naturally aligned to the size of the operand (i.e., eight‑byte aligned for doublewords). If the address is not naturally aligned, an address‑misaligned exception or an access‑fault exception *will be generated*.  

- **Reservation set size** – An implementation may register an arbitrarily large reservation set on each LR, provided the reservation set includes **all** bytes of the addressed doubleword.  

- **Reservation uniqueness** – Executing an LR (including LR.D) invalidates any previous reservation held by the hart; a hart can hold only one reservation at a time, and an SC can pair only with the most recent LR in program order.  

- **Acquire semantics** – The LR/SC sequence can be given acquire semantics by setting the `aq` bit on the LR instruction (including LR.D).  

- **Ordering constraints on bits** – Software should not set the `rl` bit on an LR instruction unless the `aq` bit is also set; setting the `aq` bit on an LR instruction does not itself act as a fence for ordinary loads and stores unless combined with the appropriate `rl`/`aq` settings on the paired SC.  

- **Analogy with word‑size variant** – LR.D "acts analogously" to LR.W, which loads a word, sign‑extends the value in `rd`, and registers a reservation set that subsumes the addressed word. By analogy, LR.D registers a reservation set that subsumes the addressed doubleword.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: LR.D loads a doubleword from the address in rs1, writes the value to rd, and registers a reservation set that subsumes the bytes of the addressed doubleword.  
RULE 2: LR.D is defined only for RV64 implementations.  
RULE 3: The address in rs1 for LR.D must be naturally aligned to eight bytes; if the address is not naturally aligned, an address‑misaligned exception or an access‑fault exception will be generated.  
RULE 4: An implementation MAY register a reservation set of any size for LR.D provided that the set includes all bytes of the addressed doubleword.  
RULE 5: Execution of LR.D MUST invalidate any previous reservation held by the hart.  
RULE 6: A hart MUST hold at most one reservation at a time.  
RULE 7: A store‑conditional instruction can succeed only if it pairs with the most recent LR.D in program order executed by the same hart.  
RULE 8: Setting the aq bit on LR.D gives the LR/SC sequence acquire semantics.  
RULE 9: Software should not set the rl bit on LR.D unless the aq bit is also set.  
RULE 10: Setting the aq bit on LR.D does not act as a fence for ordinary loads and stores unless the paired SC also has the appropriate rl and aq bits set.  
RULE 11: LR.D registers a reservation set that subsumes the addressed doubleword, analogous to the behavior of LR.W.

- **Operation**: "LR.W loads a word from the address in rs1, places the sign‑extended value in rd, and registers a reservation set – a set of bytes that subsumes the bytes in the addressed word."  

- **Sign‑extension on RV64**: "For RV64, LR.W … sign‑extend the value placed in rd."  

- **Alignment requirement**: "For LR and SC, the Zalrsc extension requires that the address held in rs1 be naturally aligned to the size of the operand (… four‑byte aligned for words). If the address is not naturally aligned, an address‑misaligned exception or an access‑fault exception will be generated."  

- **Misaligned‑access fault**: "The access‑fault exception can be generated for a memory access that would otherwise be able to complete except for the misalignment, if the misaligned access should not be emulated."  

- **Reservation set size**: "An implementation can register an arbitrarily large reservation set on each LR, provided the reservation set includes all bytes of the addressed data word or doubleword."  

- **Acquire semantics**: "The LR/SC sequence can be given acquire semantics by setting the aq bit on the LR instruction."  

- **Software constraint on rl bit**: "Software should not set the rl bit on an LR instruction unless the aq bit is also set."
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: LR.W MUST load a word from the address in rs1, place the sign‑extended value into rd, and register a reservation set that includes at least the bytes of the addressed word.  
RULE 2: On RV64 implementations, LR.W MUST sign‑extend the loaded 32‑bit value before writing it to rd.  
RULE 3: LR.W MUST cause an address‑misaligned exception or an access‑fault exception if the address in rs1 is not naturally aligned to a four‑byte boundary.  
RULE 4: If a misaligned LR.W access is not emulated, the implementation MAY raise an access‑fault exception instead of completing the load.  
RULE 5: LR.W MAY register an arbitrarily large reservation set, provided the set includes all bytes of the accessed word.  
RULE 6: LR.W can be given acquire semantics by setting its aq bit.  
RULE 7: Software SHOULD NOT set the rl bit on LR.W unless the aq bit is also set.

The following description:

- **LUI (load upper immediate)**  
  - LUI is used to build 32‑bit constants and uses the U‑type format.  
  - LUI places the 32‑bit U‑immediate value into the destination register rd, filling in the lowest 12 bits with zeros.  

- **Assembly syntax**

RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================

RULE 2: LUI writes to the destination register rd a 32‑bit value whose upper 20 bits equal the instruction's immediate field and whose lower 12 bits are set to zero.  
RULE 3: Because LUI always sets the lower 12 bits of rd to zero, the assembly syntax for LUI does not represent those bits.

The following description:

- A **LUI** instruction can first load `rs1` with the upper 20 bits of a target address, then `JALR` can add in the lower bits.  

- **LUI** may be used in macro‑op fusion sequences such as

  lui ra, imm20
  jalr ra, imm12(ra)

RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================

RULE 2: After a LUI instruction has loaded a register with its upper‑immediate value, a subsequent JALR that uses that register as its base may add the signed 12‑bit immediate to the register value to compute the jump target address.  
RULE 3: A LUI instruction may be placed immediately before a JALR instruction to form a macro‑op fusion sequence, while each instruction retains its defined architectural effect.  
RULE 4: The macro‑op fusion pattern that may involve a LUI followed by a JALR may also be formed with an AUIPC followed by a JALR.

The following description:

- **Instruction encoding and addressing**  
  - LW is a load instruction encoded in the I‑type format.  
  - The effective address is obtained by adding register **rs1** to the sign‑extended 12‑bit offset.  

- **Operation**  
  - "The LW instruction loads a 32‑bit value from memory into **rd**."  

- **Destination register x0**  
  - "Loads with a destination of **x0** must still raise any exceptions and cause any other side effects even though the load value is discarded."  

- **Endianness (byte‑address invariant)**  
  - In a little‑endian configuration, "Loads similarly transfer the contents of the lesser memory byte addresses to the less‑significant register bytes."  
  - In a big‑endian configuration, "Loads similarly transfer the contents of the greater memory byte addresses to the less‑significant register bytes."  

- **Alignment and misaligned accesses**  
  - "Regardless of EEI, loads and stores whose effective addresses are naturally aligned shall not raise an address‑misaligned exception."  
  - For LW, natural alignment means the effective address is divisible by the size of the access in bytes (4 bytes).  
  - "Loads and stores whose effective address is not naturally aligned to the referenced datatype … have behavior dependent on the EEI."  
  - An EEI may guarantee that misaligned loads are fully supported, in which case the misaligned LW can be handled in hardware, via an invisible trap, or a combination thereof.  
  - If an EEI does not guarantee invisible handling, a misaligned LW may either complete successfully or raise an exception, which can be either an **address‑misaligned exception** or an **access‑fault exception**.  
  - When an EEI does not guarantee invisible handling, the EEI "must define if exceptions caused by address misalignment result in a contained trap … or a fatal trap."  

- **Atomicity**  
  - "Whereas naturally aligned loads and stores are guaranteed to execute atomically, misaligned loads and stores might not …"  
  - Therefore a naturally aligned LW (address divisible by 4) is guaranteed to be atomic.  

- **Execution‑environment restrictions**  
  - "The EEI will define what portions of the address space are legal to access with which instructions (e.g., some addresses might be read only, or support word access only)."  
  - LW must respect those EEI‑defined permissions.

RULE 2: LW MUST load a 32‑bit value from the memory location given by its effective address into the destination register rd.  
RULE 3: LW with destination register x0 MUST still raise any applicable exceptions and perform all side effects even though the loaded value is discarded.  
RULE 4: In a little‑endian configuration, LW MUST transfer the byte from the lowest memory address of the accessed word into the least‑significant byte of rd and similarly for the remaining bytes.  
RULE 5: In a big‑endian configuration, LW MUST transfer the byte from the highest memory address of the accessed word into the least‑significant byte of rd and similarly for the remaining bytes.  
RULE 6: LW whose effective address is naturally aligned (i.e., divisible by 4) shall not raise an address‑misaligned exception regardless of the execution‑environment identifier (EEI).  
RULE 7: Natural alignment for LW is defined as an effective address that is divisible by the access size of 4 bytes.  
RULE 8: LW whose effective address is not naturally aligned SHALL have its behavior determined by the EEI.  
RULE 9: If the EEI guarantees that misaligned loads are fully supported, a misaligned LW MAY be performed entirely in hardware, MAY be handled by an invisible trap, or MAY use a combination of both mechanisms.  
RULE 10: If the EEI does not guarantee invisible handling, a misaligned LW MAY either complete successfully or raise either an address‑misaligned exception or an access‑fault exception.  
RULE 11: When the EEI does not guarantee invisible handling, the EEI MUST specify whether exceptions caused by address misalignment for LW result in a contained trap or a fatal trap.  
RULE 12: LW with a naturally aligned effective address (address divisible by 4) is guaranteed to execute atomically.  
RULE 13: LW MUST obey the permissions and address‑space restrictions defined by the EEI, such as read‑only regions or regions that only allow word accesses.

The following description:

- In the **cm.pop** operation, when **XLEN = 32** the pseudocode specifies the execution of the assembly statement  

  ```
  asm("lw x[i], 0(addr)");
  ```  

  which **loads a 32‑bit word from memory address `addr` into register `x[i]`**.

- The address used for the load is calculated as  

  `addr = sp + stack_adj – bytes`  

  where `bytes = 4` for XLEN = 32 (the size of a word loaded by **LW**).

- For each register `i` that appears in `xreg_list`, the pseudocode performs the **LW** load, then decrements the address:  

  `addr = addr – bytes` (i.e., `addr = addr – 4`).  

  This sequence is repeated for all registers listed in `xreg_list`.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: When XLEN = 32, the LW instruction must load a 32‑bit word from the memory address calculated as sp + stack_adj – 4 into the specified integer register x[i].  
RULE 2: The LW instruction must treat the value 4 as the number of bytes that constitute the word it loads when XLEN = 32.  
RULE 3: After executing LW for a register in xreg_list, the address used for the next LW must be decremented by 4 bytes.  
RULE 4: The LW instruction must be performed once for each register listed in xreg_list, using the current address before it is decremented.  
RULE 5: The address used by each LW must be updated by subtracting 4 bytes after the load completes, so that subsequent LW operations use the new address.

The following description:

- **Operation**: In the pseudocode for the `cm.popret` instruction, when `XLEN == 32` the statement `asm("lw x[i], 0(addr)");` specifies that the **LW** instruction *loads* a 32‑bit word from memory at address `addr` into integer register `x[i]`.

RULE 2: For a 32‑bit load performed by LW, the effective address is calculated as sp + stack_adj − 4, and after each LW execution the address operand for the next iteration is decremented by 4.  
RULE 3: An LW instruction may raise an exception or interrupt if the memory access at its effective address causes a fault.  
RULE 4: If an LW instruction raises an exception or interrupt, the load loop is terminated and subsequent adjustments of sp and the return operation are not performed.  
RULE 5: The load loop containing LW instructions repeats until every LW in the sequence completes without raising an exception or interrupt.

Offset** field that replaces the instruction's **rs1** field in bits 19:15 is the positive difference between the faulting virtual address (written to **mtval** or **stval**) and the original virtual address. This difference can be non‑zero only for a misaligned memory access.*  

  *For basic loads, the transformations replace the instruction's immediate offset fields with zero.*

- **Compressed‑instruction handling**  
  *Bits 1:0 of a transformed standard instruction will be binary 01 if the trapping instruction is compressed and 11 if not.*

  | Value (RV32) | Value (RV64) | Meaning |
  |--------------|--------------|---------|
  | 0x00002003   | 0x00003003   | **lw x0,0(x0)** |

The following description:

- **Instruction name**: AMOMAX.W/D (signed integer maximum) and AMOMAXU.W/D (unsigned integer maximum) are part of the "Zaamo" extension for atomic memory operations.

- **General AMO behavior applied to MAX**:  
  *"These AMO instructions atomically load a data value from the address in rs1, place the value into register rd, apply a binary operator to the loaded value and the original value in rs2, then store the result back to the original address in rs1."*  
  For AMOMAX/AMOMAXU the binary operator is the signed (respectively unsigned) integer maximum of the loaded memory value and the value in rs2.

- **Operand size**:  
  *"AMOs can either operate on doublewords (RV64 only) or words in memory."*  
  The suffix **.W** denotes a word‑sized operation (32 bits); the suffix **.D** denotes a doubleword‑sized operation (64 bits).

- **Alignment requirement**:  
  *"the Zaamo extension requires that the address held in rs1 be naturally aligned to the size of the operand (i.e., eight‑byte aligned for doublewords and four‑byte aligned for words). If the address is not naturally aligned, an address‑misaligned exception or an access‑fault exception will be generated."*  
  The optional misaligned atomicity granule PMA may relax this requirement, in which case no alignment exception is raised provided all accessed bytes lie within the same granule.

- **Sign‑extension rule for 32‑bit AMOs on RV64**:  
  *"For RV64, 32‑bit AMOs always sign‑extend the value placed in rd, and ignore the upper 32 bits of the original value of rs2."*  
  This rule applies to AMOMAX.W as well as to AMOMAXU.W (the result stored in rd is sign‑extended, and the upper 32 bits of rs2 are ignored).

- **Ordering semantics**:  
  The aq and rl bits have the same meaning for AMOMAX/AMOMAXU as for all other AMOs:  
  *If the aq bit is set, then no later memory operations in this RISC‑V hart can be observed to take place before the AMO.*  
  *If the rl bit is set, then other RISC‑V harts will not observe the AMO before memory accesses preceding the AMO in this hart.*  
  *Setting both aq and rl makes the sequence sequentially consistent.*

- **Result handling**:  
  The value loaded from memory is placed in rd; the destination register may be x0 if the return value is to be discarded (e.g., when using the AMO for a parallel reduction).

- **Exception behavior**:  
  Misaligned addresses generate an address‑misaligned exception or an access‑fault exception (unless the misaligned atomicity granule PMA applies). No other exceptions specific to MAX are described.

- **Summary of architectural effect for AMOMAX/AMOMAXU**:  
  1. Atomically read the memory word/doubleword at the address in rs1.  
  2. Write that value to rd (sign‑extended for 32‑bit operations on RV64).  
  3. Compute the signed (AMOMAX) or unsigned (AMOMAXU) maximum of the loaded value and the value in rs2.  
  4. Store the computed maximum back to the same address in rs1.  
  5. Apply any requested acquire/release ordering via the aq/rl bits.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: AMOMAX.W and AMOMAXU.W must operate on a 32‑bit word located at the address in rs1, and AMOMAX.D and AMOMAXU.D must operate on a 64‑bit doubleword located at the address in rs1.  
RULE 2: The address in rs1 used by any AMOMAX or AMOMAXU instruction must be naturally aligned to the operand size (four‑byte aligned for word operations and eight‑byte aligned for doubleword operations) unless a misaligned‑atomicity‑granule PMA applies and all accessed bytes lie within the same granule.  
RULE 3: If the address in rs1 used by an AMOMAX or AMOMAXU instruction is not naturally aligned and no applicable PMA relaxes the requirement, the implementation must raise an address‑misaligned exception or an access‑fault exception.  
RULE 4: For each execution of an AMOMAX or AMOMAXU instruction, the processor must atomically load the memory value at the address in rs1, place the loaded value into rd, compute the signed maximum for AMOMAX or the unsigned maximum for AMOMAXU of the loaded value and the value in rs2, and store the computed maximum back to the same address in rs1.  
RULE 5: For RV64 implementations, a 32‑bit AMOMAX.W or AMOMAXU.W must sign‑extend the value placed in rd and must ignore the upper 32 bits of rs2 when performing the maximum computation.  
RULE 6: If rd is x0 in an AMOMAX or AMOMAXU instruction, the loaded value is discarded while the computed maximum is still stored to memory.  
RULE 7: If the aq bit of an AMOMAX or AMOMAXU instruction is set, no later memory operation in the same hart may be observed to occur before that AMO.  
RULE 8: If the rl bit of an AMOMAX or AMOMAXU instruction is set, no other hart may observe that AMO before memory accesses that precede the AMO in the issuing hart.  
RULE 9: If both aq and rl bits are set for an AMOMAX or AMOMAXU instruction, the operation must be sequentially consistent.

The following description:

- **Operation**: FMAX.S writes the larger of the two single‑precision floating‑point operands `rs1` and `rs2` to destination register `rd`.  
- **Signed‑zero ordering**: For the purposes of FMAX.S, the value `-0.0` is considered to be less than the value `+0.0`.  
- **NaN handling**:  
  - If both inputs are NaNs, the result is the canonical NaN.  
  - If only one operand is a NaN, the result is the non‑NaN operand.  
  - Signaling NaN inputs set the *invalid operation* exception flag, even when the result is not NaN.  

*Note*: In version 2.2 of the F extension, FMAX.S was amended to implement the proposed IEEE 754‑201x *maximumNumber* operation rather than the IEEE 754‑2008 *maxNum* operation; this change concerns the handling of signaling NaNs, which is already captured by the rule that signaling NaN inputs set the invalid operation exception flag.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: MAX must write to destination register rd the larger of the two single‑precision floating‑point operands in rs1 and rs2 according to IEEE‑754 ordering.  
RULE 2: MAX must treat the value -0.0 as less than +0.0, so when the operands are -0.0 and +0.0 the result is +0.0.  
RULE 3: MAX must produce the canonical NaN as the result when both rs1 and rs2 contain NaN values.  
RULE 4: MAX must produce the non‑NaN operand as the result when exactly one of rs1 or rs2 contains a NaN value.  
RULE 5: MAX must set the invalid operation exception flag whenever any operand is a signaling NaN, even if the resulting value is not NaN.

RULE 8: For the FMAXM.Q instruction, if either source operand is a NaN, the destination register must be written with the canonical NaN.  
RULE 9: All FMAXM.* instructions must implement the IEEE 754‑2019 maximum operation, including the defined handling of signed zeros, infinities, and other special cases.

The following description:

- The **vfmax** instruction performs the *maximumNumber* operation on active elements.  
- It has the same behavior as the corresponding scalar floating‑point maximum instruction defined in version 2.2 of the RISC‑V F/D/Q extension.  
- **Forms** of the instruction:  

  | Form          | Syntax                              | Description            |
  |---------------|-------------------------------------|------------------------|
  | Vector‑vector | `vfmax.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm`         | Computes the maximum of each pair of active elements from source vectors `vs2` and `vs1`, writing the result to destination vector `vd`. |
  | Vector‑scalar | `vfmax.vf vd, vs2, rs1, vm`         | Computes the maximum of each active element of source vector `vs2` and the scalar value in integer register `rs1`, writing the result to destination vector `vd`. |

- The operation is applied only to **active elements** as determined by the mask `vm`.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: The vfmax instruction MUST perform the maximumNumber operation on each active element.  
RULE 2: The vfmax instruction's behavior MUST be identical to the scalar floating‑point maximum instruction defined in version 2.2 of the RISC‑V F/D/Q extension.  
RULE 3: In the vector‑vector form `vfmax.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm`, the instruction MUST compute the maximum of each pair of active elements from source vectors vs2 and vs1 and write the result to the corresponding element of destination vector vd.  
RULE 4: In the vector‑scalar form `vfmax.vf vd, vs2, rs1, vm`, the instruction MUST compute the maximum of each active element of source vector vs2 and the scalar value held in integer register rs1 and write the result to the corresponding element of destination vector vd.  
RULE 5: The vfmax instruction MUST apply the operation only to elements that are active according to the mask vm, leaving the destination elements for inactive positions unchanged.

The following description:

**MAX instruction (vector integer reduction)**  

- Instruction mnemonic: **vredmax.vs**  
- Operand format: `vredmax.vs  vd, vs2, vs1, vm`  

- Architectural behavior (normative description):  

  *`vd[0] = max( vs1[0] , vs2[*] )`*  

  where `vs2[*]` denotes **all active elements** of vector register `vs2`.  

- General constraints for single‑width reduction instructions (which also apply to `vredmax.vs`):  

  * All operands and the result have the **same SEW width**.  

  * Overflows **wrap around on arithmetic sums** (this rule does not affect the max operation).
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: The vector integer reduction instruction vredmax.vs (MAX) computes vd[0] as the maximum of the scalar element vs1[0] and each active element of vector register vs2, where active elements are those selected by the current vector mask vm.  
RULE 2: The MAX reduction requires that the selected element width (SEW) of vd, vs1, and vs2 be identical.  
RULE 3: The MAX reduction does not apply the wrap‑around overflow behavior defined for arithmetic sum operations.  
RULE 4: Elements of vs2 that are not active according to the vector mask vm are excluded from the maximum comparison performed by the MAX instruction.

The following description:

**MAXU**

- **Synopsis** – Unsigned maximum  
- **Mnemonic** – `maxu rd , rs1 , rs2`  
- **Description** – This instruction returns the larger of two unsigned integers.  
- **Operation**  

  ```
  let rs1_val = X(rs1);
  let rs2_val = X(rs2);
  let result = if rs1_val < _ u rs2_val then rs2_val else rs1_val;
  X(rd) = result;
  ```

- **Included in**

  | Extension | Minimum version | Lifecycle state |
  |-----------|-----------------|-----------------|
  | Zbb (Basic bit‑manipulation) | v1.0 | Ratified |
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: MAXU reads the architectural value of source register rs1 as an unsigned integer rs1_val.  
RULE 2: MAXU reads the architectural value of source register rs2 as an unsigned integer rs2_val.  
RULE 3: MAXU compares rs1_val and rs2_val using an unsigned less‑than comparison.  
RULE 4: If the unsigned comparison determines that rs1_val is less than rs2_val, MAXU writes rs2_val into destination register rd.  
RULE 5: If the unsigned comparison determines that rs1_val is not less than rs2_val, MAXU writes rs1_val into destination register rd.  
RULE 6: MAXU does not modify any architectural state other than the destination register rd.  
RULE 7: An implementation that ratifies the Zbb (Basic bit‑manipulation) extension version v1.0 must implement MAXU with the semantics defined in these rules.

The following description:

- **Instruction encoding** – The MIN operation is represented by the AMOMIN[U].W/D entry in the AMO instruction table (see the row "AMOMIN[U].W/D" in the table of atomic memory operations).

- **Operational definition** – An AMO instruction, including MIN, **atomically loads a data value from the address in rs1, places the value into register rd, applies a binary operator to the loaded value and the original value in rs2, then stores the result back to the original address in rs1**. For MIN, the binary operator is the **signed integer minimum** (for AMOMIN) or the **unsigned integer minimum** (for AMOMINU).

- **Operand size** – AMOs can operate on doublewords (RV64 only) or words. For RV64, **32‑bit AMOs always sign‑extend the value placed in rd, and ignore the upper 32 bits of the original value of rs2**. This rule applies to MIN as it does to all AMOs.

- **Alignment requirement** – The Zaamo extension **requires that the address held in rs1 be naturally aligned to the size of the operand (i.e., eight‑byte aligned for doublewords and four‑byte aligned for words)**.  
  - **If the address is not naturally aligned, an address‑misaligned exception or an access‑fault exception will be generated.**  
  - The misaligned atomicity granule PMA may relax this requirement: if all accessed bytes lie within the same misaligned atomicity granule, **the instruction will not raise an exception for reasons of address alignment**, and it will execute atomically as a single memory operation.

- **Ordering semantics** – The **aq** (acquire) and **rl** (release) bits are optional for all AMOs, including MIN.  
  - **If the aq bit is set, then no later memory operations in this RISC‑V hart can be observed to take place before the AMO.**  
  - **If the rl bit is set, then other RISC‑V harts will not observe the AMO before memory accesses preceding the AMO in this hart.**  
  - Setting both bits makes the operation **sequentially consistent**.

- **Exception behavior** – In addition to the alignment‑related exceptions described above, MIN is subject to the same memory‑access exceptions as other AMOs (e.g., page‑fault or access‑fault exceptions) because it performs a load‑modify‑store sequence.

- **Use case** – MIN, together with the other supported binary operators (swap, add, AND, OR, XOR, maximum), is intended for multiprocessor synchronization, parallel reductions, and atomic updates to memory‑mapped device registers.

=========
